entries.title: Belgium wildfire: Rains help High Fens containment efforts
entries.summary: Firefighters continue to battle one of the worst wildfires in Belgian history near the German border. Rains and cooler temperatures are helping them bring it to heel after it ravaged an area half the size of Manhattan.
entries.content:
Belgium

Belgium wildfire: Rains help High Fens containment efforts

August 18, 2026

Firefighters continue to battle one of the worst wildfires in Belgian history near the German border. Rains and cooler temperatures are helping them bring it to heel after it ravaged an area half the size of Manhattan.

Belgian firefighters were pushing to encircle and contain the country's largest wildfire in a century.

Rain and cooler temperatures provided some natural relief against the blaze on Tuesday but also teamed up with winds to hamper air support and waterbombing operations.

The fire expanded to cover an area of around 3,000 hectares — about half the size of Manhattan in New York — by Monday.

The High Fens, or Hautes Fagnes, nature reserve is a vast expanse of boggy peatlands, pine forests and hiking trails, with parts of it difficult to access with large machinery, except from above.

What's the latest on the firefighting efforts?

"We are trying to definitively encircle the fire today," regional government spokesman Niolas Yernaux told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.

Firefighters worked through the night to try to make a crucial link-up between the eastern and northern fronts, despite difficult access conditions in the hilly and wooded area.

"We're talking about one or two kilometers, and we're on the verge of achieving it," Yernaux said.

He said that the fire was "under control and contained" in areas where firefighters could operate.

However, Yernaux said the hard-to-reach front stretching towards the German border and the town of Monschau remained a concern; much of this area is only really accessible from above. The wind and rain could delay such aerial operations, potentially until Tuesday evening, he warned.

How far from the border is the fire, what's the situation in Monschau?

Residents of Monschau have already been told to leave their homes because of the smoke hazard, with the fire roughly 2.3 kilometers (roughly 1.5 miles) from the border. Yernaux said that "strong winds" were blowing towards the east and the German frontier. 

"At the moment it's manageable," Monschau fire service spokesman Tobias Schnell told the dpa news agency. Should the winds pick up further, he said that could fan the flames in the town's direction.

He said that water tanks and other equipment had already been placed in its potential path in case it is needed. He said around 170 people were working on a three-shift rotation around the clock, and that authorities were working on the assumption the operation would last several more days at least.

Smoke has spread dozens of kilometers to the east, with major cities like Cologne and Wuppertal both warning residents of the risk of poor air quality and smoke. 

"At present the smell of the fire can be perceived throughout the city," Wuppertal's fire department warned, recommending that people close doors and windows. "A health risk cannot be ruled out."

Locals start to return, but still urged to limit movements

Villagers in places like Sourbrodt, which was evacuated at the peak of the fire over the weekend, started returning to their homes as the threat subsided on Monday evening.

Nevertheless, the local Waimes municipality asked residents to exercise continued caution.

"Residents are asked to limit travel within this area to what is strictly necessary and to act with particular vigilance and responsibility," it said. "Despite the return of evacuated residents, operations carried out by the various emergency, security and response services remain a priority and must be able to proceed under the best possible conditions."

Two villages in the Bütgenbach municipality, meanwhile, remain cleared, with conditions not yet safe there.

Wallonia's Agriculture Ministry also said on Tuesday that it would review compensation for farmers who volunteered to help with the firefighting efforts.

This is was "under review — regarding both the substance and the procedure, as well as the legal feasiblity of doing so," Agriculture Minister Anne-Catherine Dalcq's office said on Tuesday.

This followed an appeal from the presdient of the Royal Federation of Belgian Firefighters, who demanded reciprocal aid after the famers' help battling the blaze.

"Who will cover the cost of the equipment damaged during this operation? Without them, the situation would be far worse," Marc Gilbert had said in an interview with the Belga news agency.

The vast fire gathered pace just after another a few kilometers east across the German border in the Hürtgenwald forest was contained late last week.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Trump's North Korea overture triggers fears for US alliances
entries.summary: In announcing scaled back joint military drills with South Korea, the US president appears to be moving towards Pyongyang just as North Korea becomes more emboldened.
entries.content:
South Korea

Trump's North Korea overture triggers fears for US alliances

August 18, 2026

In announcing scaled back joint military drills with South Korea, the US president appears to be moving towards Pyongyang just as North Korea becomes more emboldened.

US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that he had instructed the Pentagon to limit the scale of US involvement in military exercises with South Korean units planned for this week, causing alarm among South Koreans and experts concerned at the deteriorating security situation in Northeast Asia

In a social media post, Trump said he had ordered the US to "substantially reduce" its involvement, claiming the exercises were "expensive."

Trump added that US involvement in the exercises would send a "signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea, which he said has been "unthreatening and respectful" to his presidency.

Trump's statement seemed to disregard North Korea's recent spate of missile tests, and Pyongyang threatening last Friday a "new level" of nuclear deterrence in response to the planned drills, which North Korean state media called "a rehearsal for an invasion war."

The US president also hinted that his decision was in part influenced by the South Korean government's refusal to assist in the "denuclearization" of Iran.

On Monday, Trump doubled down on his decision to limit the scope and scale of the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which started the same day, telling reporters in the White House that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un had responded to his overture for a resumption of talks.

Fraying US alliances in Asia

Paring back the annual exercise comes as Kim is emboldened by a deepening alliance with Russia. At the same time, Pyongyang in recent years has removed foundational guardrails of inter-Korean relations by officially abandoning the decades-long goal of reunification, while rewriting its constitution to designate South Korea as its principal enemy.

"The cost savings from downsizing drills are marginal, while the diplomatic benefits for relations with North Korea are doubtful," said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul.

Easley added that Kim has shown "no interest" in offers from Washington and Seoul to discuss considering scrapping North Korea's nuclear arsenal.

"Trump's recent social media posts about Kim Jong-un suggest a willingness to reengage, but North Korea is busy profiting from Russia's war against Ukraine while modernizing its own military," Easley told DW.

He added that scaling back combined defense exercises "can damage alliance coordination, slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defense and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia."

South Korea walks a fine line

Concern in South Korea has been reflected in newspaper editorials on Tuesday, with the Chosun Ilbo highlighting the importance of joint drills in safeguarding the nation from an aggressive and unpredictable neighbor and warning that Trump is risking the foundations of the alliance.

David Silbey, a professor of military history and defense policy at Cornell University in the US, pointed out in a statement that the move comes as US military forces are overstretched, with the US Navy already redirecting forces from the Pacific to the Middle East amid the Iran war.

"Reducing the commitment to the South Korean exercises probably reflects a reduction that was inevitable anyway," he writes, adding that offering Kim talks also reflects "the continuing neglect of American allies," and that Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines are all watching.

Beijing is, of course, also monitoring developments closely, albeit from a position of an adversary rather than an ally, he said.  

According to the Associated Press, Trump made the decision to pull back on exercises without consulting South Korea, and it was unclear exactly which parts of the exercises were being downsized.

On Monday, the office South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said the South would continue to "coordinate closely" with the US on "maintaining a firm combined defense posture and on their joint exercises and training."

During a regular Cabinet meeting on Tuesday, President Lee lauded the US-South Korea alliance during a and called for South Korea to bolster its own forces.

"When we build up our strengths, our value and importance as an ally will further grow," he said.

A 'victory' for Kim Jong Un?

In the US, politicians from both parties have pushed back against Trump's order on the grounds that it weakens the alliance with South Korea and benefits US adversaries.

Senator Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, described the move as, "another inane, haphazard decision by President Trump and his chaotic administration."

"Kim Jong Un has won a propaganda victory and South Korea, one of our strongest allies, has been punished for no reason beyond Trump's ego," he said in a statement.

Republican Senator Thom Tillis underlined South Korea's long military alliance with the US and argued that cutting the scale of the exercises could help Russia by enabling North Korea to send more troops to fight in Ukraine.

Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, said that the majority of ordinary South Koreans are "very concerned" about the deteriorating alliance and the implications of Trump favoring Pyongyang over Seoul.

"People are alarmed," he told DW. "Trump threatened to withdraw US forces during his first term unless South Korea paid more to keep them here, he has imposed huge tariffs on our exports to the US and now he is approaching the North in a manner that shows he wants to establish a new relationship and sign a peace treaty that ends the Korean War."

Little chance for change in Pyongyang

However, Kim added that Trump still has an ally in South Korean President Lee.

"I do not think the Lee government is at all worried or disappointed in this plan," he said. "Their policy has always been to try to reinstate friendly relations with the North, even though the North has shown no intention of reciprocating."

On Monday, Lee's office issued a statement expressing optimism for "meaningful dialogue" between Trump and Kim Jong Un, which could promote peace in the region.

However, South Korean commentator Kim said that there is no indication that Pyongyang will change its belligerent posture towards the US or South Korea.

"The last time Kim Jong Un held talks with Trump, in Vietnam in 2019, North Korea was in a position of weakness," he said.

"Today, Kim has forged a solid alliance with Russia that is bringing him military technology, energy supplies and economic assistance, while China is also reaching out to the North because it does not want to be completely out of the picture," he added.

"Right now, Kim is in a very comfortable position and you could argue that he no longer needs the US," he said. "But for most people in South Korea, it comes down to something much more basic; we just do not trust the North."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Hyrox: a global fitness sensation made in Germany
entries.summary: Founded in Germany but successful worldwide, Hyrox combines running and functional training into a unique competition format. How a German idea became an international sports phenomenon.
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

Founded in Germany but successful worldwide, Hyrox combines running and functional training into a unique competition format. How a German idea became an international sports phenomenon.

There is probably no other sport in the world that has experienced a boom like Hyrox in recent years. What started as an idea in 2017 has, within just a few years, evolved into one of the fastest-growing fitness movements in the world.

The format was developed by event organizer Christian Toetzke, communications expert Michael Trautmann, and Moritz Fürste, a former member of the German national field hockey team that won gold at the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics.

Their basic idea was very simple: to create a competition that combines the atmosphere of a running event with the intensity of functional strength training that many people know from time in the gym. Hyrox consists of eight functional stations interspersed by eight one-kilometer runs.

"People love to either challenge themselves or compete against others, take part in a contest and battle their own inner demons," Fürste told DW.

People were already doing this. Hyrox simply standardizes it as a competition format.

Hyrox gives people a new purpose

To develop their concept, the founders analyzed the global sports landscape and found that there was a gap in the market of established sports.

"Most sports — such as tennis, football or ball sports in general — are very clearly defined," explained Fürste. 

"They've all been around for hundreds of years, but the one area of the sports world that was never really defined was the world of the gym. We wanted to give these people a goal to train for, aside from being healthy or looking good in the mirror."

Hyrox is not the only attempt at creating competition around gym work. CrossFit is perhaps its most famous rival. It started back in 2007, changes daily and features Olympic weightlifting and gymnastics. Hyrox is the same each time, offering more functional fitness development. The closest in style to Hyrox is DEKA Fit, although the latter's global reach is affected by its focus on local US affiliate gyms.

For Fürste, the definition of success is what happens at the end of races.

"No one finishes a race with any energy left; everyone is completely exhausted. But everyone thinks about being faster next time," Fürste said.

Clearly, Hyrox isn't the only way to train, but Fürste believes it is a good way to train for competition.

The standardized format means that events are comparable worldwide, regardless of whether you compete in Hamburg, London, New York, or Sydney. As a result, there has been a surge in interest in recent years.

Hyrox growing 100% in all markets

In a 2025 interview with "Sports Illustrated," Fürste spoke of two pivotal moments for Hyrox; first, when 650 participants turned out for their first ever event and second, when they sold out an event in London in 2022, after the pandemic. It was clear then that they were on to something.

In the 2022–23 season, around 90,000 athletes took part in Hyrox competitions. By 2025, that number had already risen to more than 650,000.

"No matter where we've gone so far, we've seen tremendous growth in the first two to three years," Fürste said.

"There wasn't a single market that didn't grow by 100% from one event to the next. This shows that the product works. It's a great experience for those who take part."

Next stop: the 2032 Olympic Games

With more than a million athletes set to compete in Hyrox events worldwide this season, it looks like there's no sign of the boom ending anytime soon.

"This shows that we're neither a trend nor a niche," Fürste said. "It shows that we've made our mark in the sports world."

Hyrox is now present in more than 85 cities in around 30 countries across the world. Studies confirm the series' extraordinary growth, with more than 278,000 finishers recorded by the end of the 2023-24 season alone.

"I invested a lot and met with people who have been working in the industry for years," said Fürste, who believes Hyrox is like the modern sports version of a music festival.

"I had to risk everything to get where I am now and to be part of this team."

While he never doubted Hyrox's success, he also never imagined it would become so big. And now the next goal looms on the horizon. Fürste told "Sports Illustrated" that he aims to make Hyrox part of the Olympic program in Brisbane in 2032, taking the popular fitness event to the world's biggest sporting stage.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Ukraine, Russia trade strikes; Wildberries site hit again
entries.summary: Ukriane reported 10 dead in a missile strike in the northeastern Kharkiv oblast near the border. Russia, meanwhile, reported more than 600 drones approaching the Moscow area and warned the UK on suppyling drones to Kyiv.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Ukraine, Russia trade strikes; Wildberries site hit again

August 18, 2026

Ukriane reported 10 dead in a missile strike in the northeastern Kharkiv oblast near the border. Russia, meanwhile, reported more than 600 drones approaching the Moscow area and warned the UK on suppyling drones to Kyiv.

Ukraine and Russia traded more attacks overnight, with the Kharkiv regional governor reporting 10 dead civilians not far from the Russian border and the Moscow mayor saying Ukraine launched some 620 drones toward the region. 

This follows one of the largest Ukrainian attacks on Russia during the war over the weekend, and the UN warning that amplified Russian strikes on towns and cities in July meant that civilian deaths in the conflict rose to levels not seen since May 2022 and the earliest months of combat.

The drone attacks on the Moscow area again caused minor damage at a facility belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries, a frequent target for Ukrainian forces of late. 

What happened in the Kharkiv missile strike?

The governor of the Kharkiv oblast, Oleh Syniehubov, on Tuesday said that the 10 people were killed and 18 more wounded in a Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenihy.

"The strike damaged 10 private houses, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars," Syniehubov wrote on Telegram, noting that the casualty figures were preliminary.

He said emergency services were responding and dealing with the attack.

Parts of the Kharkiv region in northeastern Ukraine are occupied by Russian forces. Both Kharkiv and the Belgorod region across the border in Russia have been targeted frequently throughout the war.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack targeted a busy intersection.

What happened as hundreds of drones approached Moscow?

Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that some 620 drones had flown towards the capital region overnight. He said that most were intercepted on approach, and another 180 were shot down over the Moscow area.

Russian state news agency TASS called it the heaviest such attack in two years. Russia's Defense Ministry said that, in total, it repelled 791 Ukrainian drones overnight across Russian territoy and the annexed Crimean Peninsula. The figures cannot be verified but indicate the intensity of Ukrainian strikes into Russian territory in recent days.

Moscow's regional governor, Andrei Vorobyov, issued more details on the damage caused by the drones shot down over the capital, giving a slightly lower figure of "over 150."

He said that three people were injured in three separate districts, including a young girl with a shrapnel wound to the hand.

Vorobyov also reported damage to several mainly residential buildings, including one house that "burned down completely in the village of Kuznetsy."

He said that a drone also struck a "Wildberries warehouse near Atlant-Park" in the city of Kolomna, which also logged damage at a retail site near a shopping center.

What did Russia say about reports of UK drones being used in strikes on its territory?

Russia's Embassy in London also turned its attention to drone attacks this week, responding critically on Monday evening to reports in newspaper The Times saying that drones supplied by the UK had been used in attacks on Russian territory.

The embassy asserted that such reports "confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace."

It accused the UK of "acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis," and said that "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer."

What did Germany's environment minister say during his visit to Kyiv?

Also on Tuesday, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider traveled to Kyiv. 

The Social Democrat (SPD) politician planned to spend several days in the country this week if circumstances allow.

"The goal of the trip is to work with our Ukrainian partners to identify, at an early stage, opportunities for a climate-friendly, resilient renewal of infrastructure and further reconstruction, including with the participation of the German business community," the Envirnoment Ministry said on Tuesday as Schneider was arriving.

The minister was accompanied by business representatives, not least from companies specializing in climate-friendly technologies.

Schneider also planned to be briefed on the situation for Ukraine's nuclear power plants, including the damage to protective dome covering the Chernobyl or Chornobyl reactor that melted down in the 1980s during the Soviet era.

"Its repair is highly complex," the ministry said.

Ukraine's main functioning nuclear power plant at Zaporizhzhia, meanwhile, has been under Russian military occupation and operational control since the first weeks of the war in 2022. Its reactors are in cold shutdown status but the plant still requires external power, cooling and maitenance. Close to the front lines, the plant and the surrounding area has fairly frequently come under fire. 

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Pakistan top court orders Imran Khan moved from jail to hospital
entries.summary: The former Pakistani prime minister's family has repeatedly raised concerns about his deteriorating health in prison. The 73-year-old was jailed in 2023 on corruption charges that he says were politically motivated.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan top court orders ex-PM Khan moved to hospital

August 18, 2026

The former Pakistani prime minister's family has repeatedly raised concerns about his deteriorating health in prison. The 73-year-old was jailed in 2023 on corruption charges that he says were politically motivated.

Pakistan's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered that jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan be moved to hospital for medical checks after his lawyers filed a petition citing poor health.

The top court said the 73-year-old would be transferred to Shifa International hospital in the capital, Islamabad, within two days.

The cricketer-turned-politician was jailed in 2023 after being convicted on a string of charges that he claims were politically motivated.

Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), and his family have repeatedly raised fears about his health in prison. His lawyers have also stated that he has lost most of the vision in his right eye.

Khan ally welcomes decision

Tuesday's order came after a medical team examined Khan at Rawalpnidi's Adiala jail last week, where it recorded high blood pressure, palpitations and anxiety.

"It's a very welcome order and we wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much," Sayed Zulfikar Bukhari, a close Khan aide, said in a statement.

"He should remain in hospital until all doctors are satisfied," he added.

Khan's spokesperson said he was expected to remain in hospital until September 16.

Why is Khan in jail?

Khan was Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022. Following his ouster in a no-confidence vote, he was convicted on a number of charges including allegations of an unlawful marriage and corruption. He was sentenced late last year, along with his wife, to 17 years in prison for graft.

Both deny wrongdoing.

PTI still enjoys significant support across key provinces in Pakistan, and Khan himself remains a popular figure. His arrest in early 2023 triggered nationwide protests that resulted in hundreds of people being arrested. 

Earlier this year, cricket greats from around the world appealed to the Pakistani government for Khan to receive proper medical treatment in prison, calling in a letter for "decency and justice."

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Zambia's election marred by irregularities and 'militia' arrests
entries.summary: Zambia is gripped by allegations of armed plots, intimidation and electoral interference. As President Hakainde Hichilema leads the count, concerns are growing over the state of the country's democracy.
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambia's election: irregularities and 'militia' arrests

August 18, 2026

Zambia is gripped by allegations of armed plots, intimidation and electoral interference. As President Hakainde Hichilema leads the count, concerns are growing over the state of the country's democracy.

Zambia's government announced on Sunday that police had arrested 11 people, including six opposition figures, in a raid against "militia activity." The arrests took place on Thursday night, according to a government statement.

"The individuals in issue were found in possession of high-grade military weapons, ammunition and other materials for use in armed insurrection," it said.

Zambia's main opposition party, the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Progress (NRPUP), said shots were fired in the raid, which took place at the home of its presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, as Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported.

The party said it "rejects with absolute disdain the spurious and entirely false claims made by the Zambian Government that the NRPUP, its leadership or its members have been involved in insurgency, militia activity or any related conduct whatsoever."

Mundubile added that heavily ​armed ‌personnel had raided his residence after the election in what he described as an attack on his life.

He also claimed on social media that he was interrogated by army officers over videos he had released, and that he suffered mistreatment while in custody — accusations denied by the authorities.

The government has responded that those claims were "unsubstantiated," with outgoing Minister of Foreign Affairs Mulambo Haimbe telling DW that "the individuals that have been apprehended have been charged, first of all, and will face trial."

"So, it is not Mr Mundubile's place to make assertions on matters that will go through a court process," Haimbe stressed, adding that any actions taken by authorities were to make sure that the "security of the nation is not compromized" during the election process.

Concerns raised during Zambia vote counting

The arrests come amid an intensely contested election: The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) suspended vote counting for around six hours on Friday following reports of violence perpetrated against polling staff and the alleged theft of ballot papers.

The count resumed after the commission announced that the "security threat" had eventually been contained, AFP reported.

Mundubile argued that this suspension created opportunities for interference and manipulation of results, while the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) rejected the claims, saying he was attempting to undermine public confidence in the electoral process.

Opposition figures say, however, that the concerns extend beyond the pause in the vote count.

In a statement, Makebi Zulu, vice presidential candidate of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance (TPA), alleged a broader pattern of interference involving electoral officials, missing polling documents, security force involvement and intimidation of opposition actors.

"A climate of fear cannot produce a free and fair election," Zulu warned.

Bishops demand accountability

Similar concerns have also been raised by Zambia's Conference of Catholic Bishops, which called on the ECZ to "account fully and publicly for the chain of custody of every affected ballot box and ballot paper."

The group of bishops, which wields considerable influence in the country, further urged authorities to ensure that any military deployment remain limited, transparent and temporary.

They also expressed concern over reports of harassment and the alleged detention of opposition officials by armed officers, calling for full transparency over the whereabouts of anyone held by authorities.

"Any person held by state agencies must be promptly accounted for, granted access to legal counsel and family, and either charged according to law or released," the bishops said.

EU observers: election campaign held in 'a constrained democratic space'

International observers from the European Union and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) also voiced their concerns about aspects of the electoral process, including mounting reports of intimidation and tensions surrounding the counting process.

SADC warned that the suspension of vote counting had generated "uncertainty and anxiety" among voters and political stakeholders.

The European Union Election Observation Mission raised similar concerns, saying the campaign had been held in a "constrained democratic space," also citing reports of intimidation of opposition candidates, disruptions to some rallies, late changes to electoral laws and an uneven playing field, which it said favored the ruling party.

EU chief observer Michael McNamara also pointed to incumbency advantages and heavily pro-government state media coverage, arguing that key democratic freedoms had been restricted during the campaign.

The legacy of Edgar Lungu

This increasingly polarized political landscape in Zambia is shaped largely by the last transfer of power, which brought President Hakainde Hichilema to office in 2021 after his victory over former President Edgar Lungu.

Since then, supporters of the former ruling Patriotic Front (PF) have accused the government of targeting Lungu allies through arrests and investigations, while the government has argued it is pursuing accountability after years of alleged corruption and abuse of power under the PF administration.

Lungu died in South Africa last year, resulting in growing veneration among his followers and supporters.

Cabinet Secretary Patrick Kangwa meanwhile said those taken into custody during the raids also included Patrick Mwansa, the husband of former President Lungu's daughter Tasila, who he said was being held at a police station in Lusaka.

Optimism while waiting for final results

The election results have stirred a mix of hope, anxiety and strong reactions among Zambians.

Gracious Kaoma, a political science student at the University of Zambia, said she was "very hopeful yet concerned" about the election "because the process has been unusually long and very challenging."

She added that the violence surrounding the vote had been "painful to watch." Kaoma nevertheless expressed hope that Zambia's political leaders would "reconcile and put Zambia's needs first."

Haimbe echoed those sentiments, telling DW that Zambia is "a bastion of democracy on the African continent, and it is our intention as the UPND administration of President Hakainde Hichilema to grow from strength to strength in that regard."

Meanwhile, Lusaka resident Lydia Zulu also expressed support for the incumbent leader, saying she was "happy that the elections have gone on peacefully and well. Because I have seen President Hakainde Hichilema is leading, I'm happy that he's coming back."

Final results are yet to be released, but according to the official tally, Hichilema appears to have widened his lead: ECZ figures from 70 of 226 constituencies show the incumbent ahead with 626,434 votes to challenger Brian Mundubile's 505,795 — a margin of more than 120,000 votes.

While the outcome remains undecided for now, Mundubile has repeated his allegation of widespread irregularities, claiming victory based on his party's own vote count.

Electoral authorities, howver, have rejected those claims, stressing that only the ECZ can officially declare the election result.

Kathy Short in Lusaka contributed reporting

Editors: Keith Walker and Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Fact check: How do I spot propaganda?
entries.summary: Across the world, politicians use propaganda to manipulate the thoughts and actions of others. It's a strategy deployed by democracies and dictatorships alike. How, then, can I detect propaganda?
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

Across the world, politicians use propaganda to manipulate the thoughts and actions of others. It's a strategy deployed by democracies and dictatorships alike. How, then, can I detect propaganda?

The 2026 US-Iran war was not just fought on the battlefield, but also across social media.  

AI-generated animations inspired by "The Lego Movie" showcased Iran's military power, while another animated video depicted a supersized version of US Vice President JD Vance rampaging through Tehran like Godzilla.

Accounts sharing this kind of content have amassed millions of views and offer a powerful example of propaganda in the age of artificial intelligence.

They also illustrate how propaganda, while far from a new phenomenon, continues to evolve alongside technology.

So, what is propaganda? And how can you spot it?

DW Fact check offers tips to help you navigate today's information landscape. 

Defining propaganda

Propaganda is often described as the deliberate use of information by governments, politicians and other actors to shape people’s beliefs, attitudes or behavior. 

It relies on the selective presentation of information, emphasizing certain facts while omitting or misrepresenting others.

Propaganda is not only deployed by authoritarian countries like Russia, China and North Korea; it can be found all over the world.

A key difference between systems is that propaganda in authoritarian states is often heavily centralized and tightly controlled.

In democratic societies, propaganda is often more pluralistic, produced by a wider range of actors.

Moreover, freely accessing alternative media outlets and information is far more straightforward in democracies.

What is the purpose of propaganda?

Talking to DW, Piers Robinson, a political scientist with the Organisation for Propaganda Studies, said propaganda can persuade someone to act or behave in a particular way.

He cited the example of how US politicians worked to convince the public to support the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

"In that case, famously, they exaggerated intelligence about weapons of mass destruction to make Iraq appear a bigger threat than it really was," said Robinson.

No weapons of mass destruction were ever found in the country. Images presented by the CIA purporting to prove their existence constituted misinformation deployed for propaganda purposes.

The Iraq War demonstrates another key aim of propaganda: vilifying political opponents, rival countries, or cultures or values seen as undesirable or threatening.

US President Donald Trumpis a case in point.

Researcherswho have studied his political rhetoric point to his frequent use of name-calling as a technique for discrediting political opponents and to his use of exaggerated claims to portray undocumented immigrants disparagingly. 

Propaganda is not always negative. It's also designed to cast politicians and governments in a positive light, said Pavel Koshkin, a senior research fellow at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

In Russia, Koshkin said, state-sponsored propaganda is utilized to create a "democratic image of Russia."

What role do media outlets play in spreading propaganda?

Media organizations can spread and amplify propaganda messages either knowingly or by mistake, Christian Mihr of Reporters Without Borders (RSF) told DW.

Russian state-funded broadcaster RT, for instance, is often accused of serving as a Kremlin mouthpiece. Its coverage largely reflects the Russian government's official position.

Ideally, media organizations play the opposite role: as watchdogs to sniff out and debunk propaganda.

Indeed, media researchers say this is one of the most important tasks expected of journalists.

RSF's Mihr said journalists are in an ideal position to help contextualize political propaganda by asking lawmakers tough questions and interviewing independent experts.

And what about AI-fueled propaganda?

Artificial intelligence is dramatically changing the way propaganda is created and distributed.

While producing propaganda once required hours or days of work, AI tools can now generate images, videos and audios in minutes.

This allows governments and other actors to adapt messages quickly and tailor them to different audiences, platforms and languages.

That's where the term "slopaganda" comes in. It combines propaganda and slop, a term often used for low-quality, AI-generated material.

Consider the AI-generated images mentioned above that circulated during the 2026 US-Iran war.

Their widespread use has led some observers to describe the conflict as a "slopaganda war", highlighting the emergence of a new form of online information warfare.

So, with all this in mind, how can you tell whether you’re looking at propaganda?

Tips to detect propaganda

Although propaganda is often subtle, there are, nevertheless, ways of identifying it.

One of the most effective ways is to look closely at where the information comes from.

Did a government official or agency publish the message? Does it come from a state-funded media outlet? Or from an account linked to one?

Take a moment to learn more about the source.

Who runs the source? Is there a disclosure included somewhere? Can I find information about how it is funded? Is its purpose clear?

The more information you can find out, the better you will be able to evaluate a source. And don’t forget: a lack of transparency is often a red flag.

Once you've analyzed where the information comes from, it's time to look at the content itself.

Be wary of information that provokes strong emotions, both positive and negative. Propaganda and "slopaganda” are often designed to trigger emotional reactions rather than encourage critical thinking.

Take a moment to pause if a post makes you feel angry, fearful or outraged. Or if it appeals strongly to your personal, religious, ethnic or national identity.

In addition, look carefully at what the post actually says. Reading about the topic, consulting independent sources and comparing different perspectives can help you assess a message critically.

Ask yourself the following questions:

  • Is the post presenting complex issues in simple, black-or-white terms?
  • Is it claiming that only one viewpoint is acceptable?
  • Is it demonizing groups or opponents?
  • Is it using facts selectively and leaving out important context?
  • Is it using statistics in a misleading way?

Finally, be skeptical of volume. As we saw above, "slopaganda" relies on spreading large amounts of low-quality, emotionally charged content.

One of its aims is to create the impression of consensus: the more often people see a message, the more likely they may be to perceive it as widely accepted.

So if you repeatedly see a message or come across the same claim, take a step back and investigate further.

This article was first published in 2022 and has been revised to incorporate new developments and trends. The experts featured were interviewed for the original article, and their insights continue to provide valuable context for the issues discussed.

This article is part of a DW Fact check series on digital literacy. Other articles include:

And here you can read more about how DW fact-checks fake news.

Edited by Josh Axelrod.

entries.title: Do not inhale! How wildfire smoke 'affects the whole body'
entries.summary: Wildfires destroy lives and livelihoods. But survivors and firefighters also suffer long-term harm to their health. A growing body of research suggests particulate matter (PM2.5) in wildfire smoke is a major culprit.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Do not inhale! How wildfire smoke 'affects the whole body'

Published February 23, 2026last updated August 18, 2026

Wildfires destroy lives and livelihoods. But survivors and firefighters also suffer long-term harm to their health. A growing body of research suggests particulate matter (PM2.5) in wildfire smoke is a major culprit.

Researchers are beginning to understand the long-term impact of wildfire smoke exposure on human health. And it's not good. "Your whole body is affected," said Yang Liu, Professor of Environmental Health at Emory University in Atlanta. "Wildfire smoke causes oxidative stress to your system and exacerbates or accelerates the development of diseases."

In a study published in January 2026, Yang Liu and other researchers found that repeated exposure to even moderate amounts of smoke increases the risk of stroke among older adults.

A month later, another study found that long-term exposure to wildfire smoke had contributed to an average of 24,100 deaths a year in the United States between 2006 and 2020.

Wildfire smoke contains a mixture of hazardous air pollutants. But one of the most aggressive components appears to be tiny specks of particulate matter, known as PM2.5.

PM2.5 is made up of soot, dust, and other substances that act like sponges, binding toxic metals and organic compounds to them.

If inhaled, PM2.5 particles can get into the lungs and bloodstream, from where they cause inflammation and damage to various other organs in the body.

Long-term exposure to PM2.5 has been linked to lung diseases like asthma, as well as heart disease, diabetes, dementia, and cancer.

Wildfire smoke is particularly dangerous for pregnant women. It can increase the risk of premature births and low birth weight. 

What makes PM2.5 in wildfire smoke so toxic

Wildfire PM2.5 is particularly toxic due to complex mixtures of burning materials found at any site, which can differ between rural fires and those that spread to urban areas.

"It really does depend on the location of the fire. It might even vary from block to block — the smoke may consist of different components," said Mary Johnson, a principal research scientist in the Department of Environmental Health at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

Johnson led an international team that studied toxic substances in wildfire smoke in a group of healthy firefighters and civilians who had recently been exposed to wildfire smoke. They wanted to understand how these toxins disrupt immune cell function and increase the body's susceptibility to infections and chronic diseases.

The researchers found mercury and cadmium — both heavy metals found naturally in plants and soils, as well as in man-made materials. They also found carcinogenic compounds and so-called forever chemicals, known as PFAS.

PFAS are synthetic chemicals used in many everyday products and building materials. They have been linked to various cancers and metabolic conditions.

Their findings led them to suggest future research should focus on developing treatments for vulnerable groups like children and elderly people and those with chronic health conditions.

Wildfire smoke becomes more toxic over time and distance

Wildfire smoke becomes more dangerous as it ages, undergoing chemical reactions that increase its ability to damage cells.

Researchers in Greece found that smoke can get up to four times more toxic in the days following a fire. It can also travel long distances quickly and spread to areas thousands of miles away from the original source of the fire. 

"If there is no rain to wash out these particles, they can stay in the atmosphere for ten days or sometimes more. They can go around the whole hemisphere and come back to the departure point within this time," said Nikolaos Mihalopoulos, director of the Institute for Environmental Research and Sustainable Development at the National Observatory of Athens.

During the Canadian wildfires of 2023, for example, 6,000 fires burned 15 million hectares of land, causing "long-range PM2.5 pollution" to spread across North America and even reach Europe and Asia. 

In a paper published in September 2025, researchers estimated that about 5,400 acute deaths in North America and about 64,300 chronic deaths in North America and Europe could be linked to PM2.5 exposure from the 2023 Canadian wildfires.

However, it is worth noting that other sources of air pollution — traffic exhaust fumes, industrial emissions, and burning fuel for cooking — still cause more health problems overall because people are exposed to them daily.

"When we look at what really drives mortality in the population as a whole, it's still all these other sources [of air pollution] that are really responsible for so many deaths," said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health.

How to protect yourself against wildfire smoke

Wildfire smoke is uniquely toxic, especially for people living near areas prone to fires. 

"The more you can do to minimize exposure, the better," said Johnson, who recommends staying indoors during and immediately after fires, using filters on heating and air conditioning systems, keeping N95-grade masks available, and ensuring vulnerable people have emergency supplies of medication and inhalers readily accessible.

Ahead of fire seasons, people should clear their properties of flammable materials and set up neighborhood monitoring groups that look out for early fire signs and help stop small fires from becoming catastrophic ones.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: Meta trial over social media harm to children begins
entries.summary: Four US states are taking Meta to court, accusing the social media giant of deliberately making Facebook and Instagram addictive for children. They're seeking damages and changes to the company's apps.
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

Four US states are taking Meta to court, accusing the social media giant of deliberately making Facebook and Instagram addictive for children. They're seeking damages and changes to the company's apps.

A landmark trial seeking to hold Meta accountable for the alleged harm its social media platforms cause children is set to begin in California on Tuesday.

Four US states, California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey, argue the company misled the public about the safety of Instagram and Facebook and deliberately made the apps addictive for minors.

Lawyers for the states also allege Meta is violating privacy laws by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without their parents' consent.

The states are seeking around $200 billion (€173 billion) in damages as well as significant changes to Meta's core platforms.

They are part of a coalition of 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023 for allegedly building addictive features into its apps.

What to expect during the trial

Opening statements were set to get underway in the federal court in Oakland, a short drive from San Francisco, on Tuesday.

Among the star witnesses expected to testify during the proceedings is Meta founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.

Former Meta employee and expert witness Arturo Bejar is also expected to testify, despite the company's efforts to block his appearance.

According to court documents, lawyers for the states are to question him for three hours about Meta's safety practices and whether the company publicly misrepresented what it knew.

Eight people are serving on an advisory jury, but the final decision in the case rests with Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers.

What have both sides said about the case?

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman described the case as "the largest consumer protection lawsuit in American history."

"We'll show a jury that Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people because looking away was more profitable," he said in a statement.

Meta, meanwhile, said it strongly disagreed with the allegations.

"We are proud of our record in protecting teens on our platforms and the amount of effort that we've put into developing protections over the years, even before these cases were ever filed," the company said.

"We look forward to showing the judge and the jury those facts in court," it added.

The trial is set to last six to eight weeks, with a verdict expected by October.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Germany updates: New drone research center to be opened
entries.summary: Two weeks after a drone security breach at Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is set to open a new drone research center. Meanwhile, an historic aquarium is set to reopen in Berlin. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany updates: New drone research center to be opened

Published August 18, 2026last updated August 18, 2026

Two weeks after a drone security breach at Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is set to open a new drone research center. Meanwhile, an historic aquarium is set to reopen in Berlin. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Tuesday, 18 August, 2026.

  • Ukrainian jailed in Germany over Russian sabotage plot
  • New drone research center to open in Saxony-Anhalt
  • Historic aquarium to reopen in Berlin

Skip next section German Jewish Council criticizes Israeli minister

German Jewish Council criticizes Israeli minister

The Central Council of Jews in Germany (ZdJ) has criticized remarks made by Israel's national security minister, calling them "inhuman," "shameful" and "irresponsible."

Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right extremist who has been part of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government since 2022, called in a podcast over the weekend for more "targeted killings" of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, up to "30-40 per night," including civilians who he said were "not worthy of life" and "shouldn't live" because they're "not even people."

"Ben-Gvir's inhuman comments stand diametrically opposed to Jewish values and damage the reputation of Israel," ZdJ president Josef Schuster told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA).

"Itamar Ben-Gvir's behavior is utterly shameful and irresponsible. It illustrates the danger posed by far-right forces."

Skip next section Vietnam orders probe into incident at Munich Airport

Vietnam orders probe into incident at Munich Airport

Vietnam's Ministry of Construction has ordered the country's aviation regulator and national flag carrier, Vietnam Airlines, to cooperate with German authorities investigating an incident involving a Boeing 787-9 at Munich Airport over the weekend.

On Saturday, Vietnam Airlines flight VN34 from Munich to Hanoi was forced to land back in the Bavarian capital after the aircraft issued warnings shortly after takeoff indicating a possible tail strike and abnormal tire pressure.

The plane remained in the sky above southern Germany for about two hours, dumping fuel in order to reduce the aircraft's weight before landing again. No injuries were reported among either the 271 passengers or 16 crew members.

The ministry has instructed the Civil Aviation Authority of Vietnam (CAAV) to establish official communication channels with German aviation authorities and to participate in the investigation in accordance with Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation.

The CAAV has also been ordered to improve its oversight of Vietnamese airlines and their personnel training and aircraft maintenance operations.

Skip next section Ukrainian handed jail sentence for spying for Russia; two others acquitted

Ukrainian handed jail sentence for spying for Russia; two others acquitted

A Stuttgart court has sentenced a young Ukrainian man to one year and three months in prison after being found guilty of conspiring to carry out arson attacks on behalf of Russia – but two other men have been acquitted.

The three men, aged 22, 25 and 30, were arrested in May 2025 in Cologne, Constance and Thurgau (Switzerland) on suspicion of sending packages with GPS trackers from Germany to Ukraine. The aim, according to prosecutors, was to reveal the precise transport routes and pass the information on to Russian secret services.

In a second step, the men were allegedly planning to dispatch packages which were designed to ignite while in transit, but the plan was discovered before it could be implemented.

The men were charged with spying and conspiracy to carry out arson attacks.

The prosecution has called for sentences ranging from two years and nine months to four years and three months, while the defense has argued for acquittal for all three defendants.

The case evokes memories of an incident in 2024, when an air freight package caught fire at a DHL logistics hub in Leipzig. Security sources believe the package was planted on behalf of Russia.

Just recently, in early August, a drone equipped with explosives and a detonator was discovered at Leipzig Airport near Ukrainian transport aircraft (see below).

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) described it as a "hybrid" attack by a "foreign power." Federal prosecutors are investigating.

Skip next section Historic Berlin aquarium reopens after three years

Historic Berlin aquarium reopens after three years

The historic aquarium at Berlin Zoo was officially reopened on Tuesday after three years of renovation work.

The three-floor aquarium (plus two additional floors for staff) is home to around 20,000 fish, reptiles, insects and other aquatic creatures representing 1,000 species and living in and around 1 million liters of water.

The main attractions are the 25 different types of jellyfish (the largest such collection in the world, according to the aquarium) and the historic crocodile enclosure, which was one of the original highlights when the aquarium first opened exactly 113 years ago on Aug. 18, 1913.

Back then, of course, as Germany's left-leaning TAZ newspaper points out, the German Empire was at its imperial height, when exotic animals were brought back to Europe using the same colonial routes which also enabled the transport of raw materials and even people away from conquered territories in Africa and Asia.

The Berlin aquarium's first director, Oskar Heinroth (1871-1945), remains a respected and pioneering zoologist, although the field at the time often contributed to Social Darwinist and eugenic thinking.

The aquarium was almost totally destroyed during the Second World War and was slowly rebuilt: the ground floor in 1952, the terrarium in 1956 and the insect enclosure in 1959. By 1968, the aquarium once again possessed one of the biggest collections of watery species in the world.

Today, the aquarium's inhabitants are fed in part with food grown on-site, including locusts, crickets, sea plankton and various types of flies. Even banana trees are grown in the warm attic beneath the roof.

Sometimes, the creatures receive particularly close attention when staff members, seven of whom are trained divers, enter the water to care for them. Visitors, however, are advised to stay behind the glass.

Skip next section Germany opens new drone research center

Germany opens new drone research center

A new drone research center is set to open in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday, two weeks after an incident involving a drone at an airport in nearby Leipzig.

The new facility at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) in Cochstedt, just south of the city of Magdeburg, will be officially opened by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU), Research and Technology Minister Dorothee Bär (CSU) and Saxony-Anhalt state premier Sven Schulze (CDU).

The center will conduct research into new drone security technologies and test them under realistic conditions, combining scientific theory with the practical demands of Germany's security services.

"The arms race in drone technology calls for specific research facilities in order to keep up," Dobrindt said following the recent incident in Leipzig, when an explosive-laden drone was discovered close to several Ukrainian cargo planes. State prosecutors spoke of a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure" and are continuing their investigations.

An interior ministry spokeswoman said on Monday that "a lot of research, development and observation" is required in order to determine what exactly Germany needs to improve its anti-drone capabilities, and said that the new Cochstedt facility would be a "key component" in this endeavor.

The German government is particularly concerned about developments in AI-controlled drones which can continue towards their targets even when jammers interrupt their connections. Another key aspect involves the accurate identification of different types of drones in order to implement the most effective form of defense.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag! Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Tuesday, 18 August, 2026.

A new drone research center is set to be officially opened not far from Leipzig airport, where an explosive-laden drone was recently discovered close to Ukrainian cargo planes.

Meanwhile, a court is set to deliver its verdict in the trial of three Ukrainians accused of plotting attacks on German freight transport on behalf of Russia.

And in Berlin, an historic aquarium is set to reopen.
